catalog_quote: Initially, I had thought that syllable prominence plays an important role in tone assignment in Ọ́lọ̀mà, but Ọ́lọ̀mà is not a stress language. Nevertheless, the tonal assignment and tonal prominence scale presented by de Lacy (1999:5) states that a higher tone is more prominent than a lower tone ... It appears that word-final and utterance-final positions in Ọ́lọ̀mà are ‘weaker’ positions and will not attract the prominence of the high tone. I have abandoned this strategy because I cannot prove that certain syllables are weaker or stronger in the language, but it is worth experimenting to see whether metrical phonology could provide clarity. [p. 138] ... Ọ́lọ̀mà is a terraced level tone language with two contrastive tones, High or H marked by an acute sign [ ́ ] and Low or L marked by a grave sign [ ̀ ]. Ọ́lọ̀mà has two contrastive contour tones: falling tone [ ̂ ] and rising tone [ ̌ ]…

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is a 342-page text-layer PDF (Word-produced, dated 2023-03-23, author "japhet ajani"). Re-extracted PDF p. 160 (printed p. 138) with extracted text: inside §4.2.2.4.2 "High Tone in Ọ́lọ̀mà" (heading confirmed in the TOC and body) the sentence reads exactly "Initially, I had thought that syllable prominence plays an important role in tone assignment in Ọ́lọ̀mà, but Ọ́lọ̀mà is not a stress language." The surrounding paragraph considers Franich 2021 / Liberman & Prince 1977 metrical prominence as an explanation for the ban on H in word-/utterance-final position, then says "I have abandoned this strategy because I cannot prove that certain syllables are weaker or stronger in the language",…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Oloma has no word stress: the author states outright that it is not a stress language. Word prosody is tonal (terraced-level system, two contrastive level tones H and L plus falling and rising contours). The remark comes while considering, and rejecting, a metrical (prominence-based) account of why high tones are avoided word-finally; the author says he cannot show that any syllable is metrically stronger or weaker.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The author notes only that word-final and utterance-final positions appear 'weaker' in that they do not attract high tone, but explicitly abandons a metrical-prominence explanation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tone assignment within words); the stress remark is a single explicit sentence inside a theoretical discussion of tonal asymmetry rather than a dedicated suprasegmentals subsection, but it is first-hand, from 11 months of fieldwork with 21 consultants and Praat-annotated data. No instrumental stress study.
new_statements.identity_note: Ajani 2023 describes Ọ́lọ̀mà as spoken in the Oloma community of Akoko-Edo (Edo State, Nigeria), near Ọ̀kpẹ̀ and Ghotuo; the dissertation argues Ọ́lọ̀mà and (Akoko-Edo) Ọ̀kpẹ̀ are distinct languages. This matches olom1241 directly; no dialect split is described.
